question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old man receiving his fifth cycle of infusional FOLFOX-bevacizumab for metastatic sigmoid adenocarcinoma arrived to the medical day hospital late this morning because the lower half of his left leg had grown noticeably fuller and achy since the previous evening. He drives himself to treatments and continues to work part-time as an IT consultant, typically seated at a desk for two-hour stretches before getting up to refill coffee or walk about the office; over the past week he had logged roughly 6,000–7,000 steps daily on his fitness watch, had completed a 30-minute neighborhood walk with his partner the night before the swelling began, and has not spent more than a single day confined to bed at any point during chemotherapy. He has not experienced fevers, rigors, night sweats, rash, insect bite, recent travel, prolonged flights, or trauma to the limb, and he flatly denies any prior clot in his legs or lungs. His only surgeries were a laparoscopic low anterior resection and port placement eight months ago at the time of diagnosis, both wounds now well healed; he has had no additional operations, endoscopic procedures, catheterizations, orthopedic casts, or splints within the past twelve weeks, and there have been no episodes of limb weakness or numbness since. Other medical history includes well-controlled dyspepsia on pantoprazole and mild hypertension treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily. He has never taken estrogen, testosterone, or anabolic supplements, does not smoke, drinks an occasional craft beer on weekends, and uses no recreational drugs. There is no family history of venous thromboembolism, connective-tissue disease, or early coronary events. On review of systems he notes a dull pressure that intensifies when he points the toes upward or when the examiner presses behind the knee, but no redness, pruritus, weeping skin, ankle discoloration, foot numbness, or back pain. Upon arrival—before any medications or intravenous fluids were started—vital signs read temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. He walked to the examination cot without assistance, though favoring the left side. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs or gallops; lungs were clear bilaterally. Abdomen was soft with a well-healed periumbilical port scar and no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower limbs showed a pronounced increase in girth limited to the mid-calf region on the left: at a standardized landmark 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity the tape measured 43.8 cm on the symptomatic side versus 39.5 cm on the right, a disparity of 4.3 cm. Thigh circumference 15 cm above the patella was symmetric at 50 cm, and ankle measurement around the malleoli differed by less than 1 cm. The overlying skin retained normal coloration without erythema, streaking, induration, or visible straight or lattice-like subcutaneous venous channels, and no distended collateral veins were seen. Palpation along the course of the popliteal and posterior tibial vessels elicited a discrete, reproducible soreness, whereas compressing the gastrocnemius belly laterally produced only mild, diffuse discomfort; no subcutaneous cords or nodules were appreciated. The limb was neither unusually warm nor cool compared with the contralateral side when tested with the dorsum of the examiner’s hand. Gentle thumb pressure over the anterior tibia left no persistent indentation. Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended provoked a tugging ache deep in the calf, while hip and knee ranges of motion were full and painless. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill in all toes was under two seconds, and motor strength of plantarflexion and dorsiflexion graded 5/5 without sensory deficits. No inguinal or popliteal adenopathy was detected. Baseline laboratory results drawn before any anticoagulation showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelet count 312 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 21 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds. A point-of-care urinalysis was unremarkable and electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm. Given the acute unilateral calf enlargement exceeding three centimeters, the pinpoint tenderness traced precisely over the deep venous path, the ongoing malignancy known to confer hypercoagulability, the absence of immobilization, recent surgery, or prior clotting episodes, and the lack of dermatologic or musculoskeletal findings that would favor cellulitis, Achilles rupture, or compartment syndrome, no competing diagnosis currently rivals an acute deep venous thrombosis in likelihood, so cross-sectional vascular imaging of the entire left lower extremity has been requested urgently while oncology infusion is temporarily held.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score assigns 1 point per positive risk factor or examination finding and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
• Active cancer: metastatic adenocarcinoma on chemotherapy, +1.
• Localized tenderness along the deep veins: popliteal and posterior tibial tenderness, +1.
• Calf enlargement ≥3 cm at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 43.8 − 39.5 = 4.3 cm, +1.
• Paralysis, paresis, or recent leg casting: 0. Bed rest ≥3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks: 0.
• Entire leg swollen: 0 (swelling is confined to the calf). Unilateral pitting edema: 0. Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: 0. Previous DVT: 0.
• No alternative diagnosis is at least as likely: no deduction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
